newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil state debt scandal spooks local stock mkt.
newsitem.headline: Brazil state debt scandal spooks local stock mkt.

text.p: A probe by Brazilian senators into a multi-million state debt scam has sent jitters through local stock markets and threatens to envelop some large banks and pension funds, analysts said.

Stock prices have been sliding over the past two days amid media reports that legislators looking into irregularities in the dealing of state and municipal bonds could question asset managers at some leading financial institutions which bought the bonds.

An aide to Senator Vilson Kleinubing confirmed that senators would meet next Tuesday to discuss the possibility of questioning managers at large banks and pension funds, but declined to make further comments on the reports.
"This is a delicate issue. All I can say is that they will discuss the subject when they meet Tuesday," he said.

A Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry (CPI) has been set up by the Senate to investigate allegations that brokers and officials may have siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars through suspect municipal and state bond issues.
The state debt probe centers on claims that several states and some cities sold bonds at well below market prices, ensuring instant profits for brokers and others involved in the scheme.
Local bolsas had apparently weathered the scandal even after the Central Bank last week closed more than a dozen small banks and brokerage houses suspected of involvement.
But now that large banks, which allegedly acquired municipal and state bonds for their fixed-income fund portfolios, could be asked to testify, analysts are more concerned.
"We do not know where this probe will lead," said a broker. "When in doubt, investors prefer to be cautious."

Analysts also fear that the state debt probe will lead to a broad congressional inquiry into Brazil's financial sector that would end up distracting lawmakers from the much-awaited approval of key reforms.
Press reports said the CPI wants to find out if the banks bought the bonds for their investment fund portfolios at above-market prices, causing losses to investors.
Newspapers cited Bradesco and Banco Itau, Brazil's two largest private banks, among the banks that purchased the bonds and would be asked to testify.
Spokespersons for Bradesco and Itau said the banks would be available to cooperate with senators if asked to testify.

"If needed, the bank will have every desire to cooperate with the work of the CPI," said a spokeswoman for Bradesco. Banco Itau also said it would help, even though it said it is not active in the state public bond market.
In addition to corruption claims, states and cities are accused of misusing the money raised through the bond issues.
The funds should only have been used for court settlements, but officials say that they were diverted to other purposes.
